migrationNotes: Spine: one crate moving along a plank on two posts. In the middle each post carries half, nearer one end the closer post carries more, a spread load acts as one force at its middle, and a load beyond the end pulls the far post down.

lesson.title: Reactions of a supported beam

lead.text: A beam resting on two supports does not fall because each support pushes back up on it. That upward push is called a reaction. The beam presses down on each support with the load it passes on, and by Newton's third law the support presses up with the same force. Reactions are forces we do not know in advance, and finding them is the first job in analysing any structure, since you cannot size a post until you know how much it has to carry.

The beam is at rest, so the forces on it balance. The upward reactions must add up to the downward load. With a 20 kN crate on the plank, the two reactions together make 20 kN. If the crate sits halfway along, nothing favours either support and each carries 10 kN. Slide the crate towards one end and the nearer support will carry more. The rest of this lesson works out by how much.
The crate is at the middle, so nothing favours either support.

The two supports of a beam are rarely the same kind. A pin holds the beam in place. It can push in any direction, but the beam is still free to turn about it. A roller sits on a surface like a wheel on a rail, and it can only push at right angles to that surface, which for a level beam means straight up. The beam is free to slide along a roller and to turn on it.

Engineers usually rest one end of a beam on a pin and the other on a roller. That lets the beam grow and shrink with the temperature without cracking its supports. A third kind, the fixed support, grips the beam so tightly that it cannot turn either, and it appears in a later lesson.

afterFigure.text: With only vertical loads, the pin pushes straight up too, so both supports push up. The picture shows what each kind of support can push with and how the beam may still move.

lead.text: Now put the load nearer one end, and call the left support A and the right support B. The beam is at rest, so the moments about any point must cancel as well as the forces, as the last lesson showed. The trick is to choose the point carefully. Take moments about the support at A. The reaction at A acts through A itself, so its distance from A is zero and it has no moment about A. That leaves the moment of the load and the moment of the reaction at B, which is the only unknown.

Let the beam be 8 m between supports, carrying 16 kN at 3 m from A. About A the load turns the beam one way with a moment of 16 × 3 = 48 kN·m. The reaction at B, written RB, turns it the other way with a moment of RB × 8. Balance needs 8 × RB = 48, so RB = 6 kN. The load is 16 kN in all, so the reaction at A is 16 − 6 = 10 kN.

afterFigure.text: The support nearer the load carries more, which gives a useful check on any answer. The two reactions add up to the load, and the bigger one belongs to the closer support.

lead.text: Take moments about A, so that the reaction at A drops out of the equation.

steps.headline: A load spread along the beam

lead.text: Not every load sits at one point. Sand heaped along a plank, or the weight of a floor, is spread along the beam and described by an intensity such as 2 kN/m, meaning 2 kN on every metre. A load of w kN/m over a length L has a total of w × L. At 2 kN/m over 5 m that is 10 kN.

For finding reactions, the whole spread load can be replaced by one force equal to its total, acting at the middle of the loaded length. For the 10 kN above, starting at the left support, the force acts 2.5 m along. The replacement has the same total and the same moment about any point as the spread load, so it gives the same reactions. The picture compares the two.

afterFigure.text: The shortcut applies to reactions only. Inside the beam, the bending depends on how the load is really spread, and a later lesson looks at that.

lead.text: Use the total of the load and the middle of its length.
Replace the spread load by one force first, then take moments about the left support.

Beams often stick out past a support, like a balcony or a diving board. A load out on the overhang can swing the beam about the nearer support and lift the far end, so the far support has to hold the beam down.

Count upward reactions as positive and keep the sign. Take a beam with supports at x = 0 and x = 6 m and a 9 kN load at the free end, x = 8 m. Moments about x = 0 give 6 × RB = 9 × 8, so RB = 12 kN upward. The reactions must still add up to the load, so RA + 12 = 9 and RA = −3 kN. The minus sign says the reaction at x = 0 points down. A support that could only push would let that end of the beam lift off.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows an overhanging load next to a load between the supports. A negative reaction is the sign that a load has gone beyond a support.

lead.text: Count upward as positive and keep the sign in your answer.

blocks.text: A plank is laid across a stream and rests on a bank at each end. Stand in the middle and it sags a little but holds. Walk towards one bank and the end by that bank takes more of your weight, while the far end takes less. Nobody can see that happening, yet each bank is working harder or less hard as you move.

Floor beams, bridge girders and shelves are the same arrangement. Whoever designs one has to know how much each support must carry, because that decides how strong the posts and walls under it have to be. The answer comes from the turning effects of the last lesson, and it needs no more than a little arithmetic.
This lesson follows a load as it moves along a beam. A crate starts in the middle and slides towards one end. Later the load is spread along the plank, and last of all it hangs past the end.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how much each end of a loaded beam carries, even for a spread load or an overhang.

recap.keyIdea: Take moments about one support and its reaction drops out, which gives the other reaction. Vertical balance then gives the first.

blocks.text: Back at the plank, you found that a 12 kN load 2 m from A puts 4 kN on B and 8 kN on A, and replaced a 4 kN/m load over 3 m by a single 12 kN force. A 10 kN load on an overhang pulled the near support down, giving −5 kN at A.

recap.nextHook: A truss is a frame of bars where the plank was, and the next lesson works out the force in each bar from the reactions you can now find.

questions.prompt: A 6 m plank is held up by a post at each end. A 12 kN crate sits exactly halfway along it. How much does each post carry, in kN?
hints: The crate is exactly halfway. Does either post carry more?
The two posts together must carry the whole crate.
Share the crate between the two equally.
questions.onCorrect: 6 kN each, by symmetry. What if the crate is nearer one end?

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole crate on one post. Symmetry shares it between the two.
That is only a quarter of the crate. The two posts together must carry all of it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The crate is at the middle, so by symmetry each post carries half of 12 kN.

questions.prompt: You take moments about support A. Which unknown force disappears from the equation?
hints: Where does the reaction at A act? How far is that from A?
questions.onCorrect: The reaction at A acts through A, so it has no arm and no moment about A.

misconceptions.feedback: The reaction at B acts at a distance from A, so it still has a moment about A.
The load is known, and it acts away from A, so it stays in the equation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reaction at A. The reaction at A passes through A, so its moment about A is zero.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam rests on a pin at A (x = 0) and a roller at B (x = 6 m). It carries 12 kN at x = 2 m. Take moments about A to find the reaction at B in kN.
hints: Taking moments about A removes the reaction at A from the equation.
The load's moment about A must equal B's moment about A.
Calculate 12 × 2 ÷ 6.
questions.onCorrect: 4 kN. Moments about A balance the load against RB, and the reaction at A drops out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the load's moment about A, in kN·m. Divide by the distance between the supports to get a force.
That is the reaction at A, the nearer support. Moments about A give the other one.

hints: What is the moment of a force whose line passes through the point?
questions.onCorrect: Choose the point so that an unknown force passes through it. That leaves one unknown.

misconceptions.feedback: Moments can be taken about any point. The skill is choosing the one that removes an unknown.
The load here sits at x = 1 m, not at A.

hints: The two reactions together carry the whole load.
What is the load, and how much does B take?
Calculate 12 − 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RA = 12 − RB = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Moments about B confirm it: 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. A is nearer the load, so it carries more: the reactions add up to the load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction at B. A is nearer the load, so it carries more.
That would be the share if the load sat at the middle. This load is nearer A.

questions.prompt: A load of 5 kN/m covers 4 m of a beam, starting at x = 0. Which single force replaces it when finding reactions?
hints: Total = intensity × length. Where is the middle of the loaded length?
questions.onCorrect: The total is intensity times length, acting at the middle of the loaded length.

misconceptions.feedback: The force acts at the middle of the loaded length, not at its end.
That is the intensity. The total multiplies it by the loaded length.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 20 kN at x = 2 m. 5 × 4 = 20 kN, acting at the middle of the loaded length, x = 2 m.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on supports at x = 0 and x = 6 m carries 4 kN/m over its first 3 m. Find the reaction at the right-hand support in kN.
hints: Replace the spread load by its total acting at the middle of the loaded length.
Take moments about the left support.
Calculate (4 × 3) × 1.5 ÷ 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spread load totals 4 × 3 = 12 kN acting at x = 1.5 m. About the left support: 6R = 12 × 1.5, so R = 3 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 3 kN. The spread load acts as one force at its middle, so the right support takes the smaller share.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the spread load. Its moment about the left support needs its arm at the middle of the loaded length.
That is the left reaction. The question asks for the right-hand support.
That shares the total equally, but the load sits only on the left half.

questions.prompt: A beam has supports at x = 0 and x = 4 m and a 10 kN load at its free end, x = 6 m. Taking upward as positive, find the reaction at x = 0 in kN.
hints: Find the reaction at x = 4 m first, by moments about x = 0.
Then the two reactions must add to the 10 kN load.
Calculate 10 − 10 × 6 ÷ 4, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About x = 0: 4RB = 10 × 6, so RB = 15 kN. Then RA = 10 − 15 = −5 kN: the left support pulls down.

questions.onCorrect: A negative reaction means the support holds the beam down. The overhanging load levers the far end up.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. With upward positive, a support that holds the beam down is negative.
That is the reaction at the other support. Subtract it from the load to get this one.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on supports at its ends carries 20 kN at x = 3 m and 10 kN at x = 8 m. Find the left reaction in kN.
hints: Take moments about the right-hand support to remove its reaction.
Measure each load's distance from x = 10 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About the right support: 10RA = 20 × 7 + 10 × 2 = 160, so RA = 16 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 16 kN. Moments about the far support: each load's force times its distance from it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the other reaction. The question asks for the left one.
That is the sum of the moments. Divide by the span to get a force.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on end supports carries 3 kN/m over its whole length. Find the left reaction in kN.
hints: What is the total of the spread load?
Where does the replacement force act?
The load is centred, so the supports share it equally.
questions.onCorrect: 15 kN. The spread load acts as 30 kN at the middle, shared equally by symmetry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load. Each support takes a share.
That is a quarter of the load. Each support carries half.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load totals 3 × 10 = 30 kN at the middle, so each support carries half: 15 kN.

questions.prompt: Name the support that stops a beam moving vertically but lets it slide horizontally and rotate.
hints: One support of a simply supported beam is free to slide so the beam can expand.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A roller support: it pushes at right angles to its surface and nothing more.

A fixed support stops rotation too. This one lets the beam rotate.
